Let \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) be a point-symmetric—or vertex-transitive—reflexive relation. Thus every vertex has a loop, the automorphism group of \(\Gamma\) acts transitively on \(V\), and all vertices have the same out-degree. Assume that the out-neighborhood
\[
\Gamma(v)=\{w\in V:(v,w)\in E\}
\]
is finite. For \(j\ge 0\), write \(\Gamma^j(v)\) for the set of vertices reachable from \(v\) by a directed walk of length at most \(j\); reflexivity ensures that these iterated neighborhoods form an increasing sequence. Also, let \(\Gamma^{-}(v)\) denote the in-neighborhood of \(v\).

Suppose that, for some \(j\in\mathbb N\),
\[
\Gamma^j(v)\cap \Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\}.
\]
In other words, among the vertices reachable from \(v\) within \(j\) steps, only \(v\) itself has an edge back to \(v\). Under this hypothesis, the \(j\)-th iterated neighborhood must grow by at least \(|\Gamma(v)|-1\):
\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1.
\]
Applying this estimate successively gives the linear lower bound
\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge 1+\bigl(|\Gamma(v)|-1\bigr)j.
\]
Thus, unless a short directed return to \(v\) occurs, each iteration introduces at least \(|\Gamma(v)|-1\) new vertices.

This growth estimate confirms Seymour’s recent conjecture in the vertex-symmetric setting. It also provides a short proof of the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture for vertex-symmetric directed graphs: sufficiently large out-degree forces the existence of a short directed cycle. More broadly, the result extends a classical additive theorem of Shepherdson, translating an additive expansion principle into the language of iterated neighborhoods in point-symmetric relations.

Let \(\Gamma\) be a reflexive directed relation on a set \(V\), meaning that every vertex is related to itself, and assume that \(\Gamma\) is point-symmetric (vertex-transitive) and that each vertex has a finite neighborhood. For \(v\in V\), write \(\Gamma(v)\) for its out-neighborhood, \(\Gamma^{-}(v)\) for its in-neighborhood, and \(\Gamma^{j}(v)\) for the set of vertices reachable from \(v\) in at most \(j\) steps. The authors examine the growth of these iterated neighborhoods when
\[
\Gamma^{j}(v)\cap \Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\}.
\]
Thus, apart from the reflexive loop at \(v\), no vertex that can be reached from \(v\) within \(j\) steps has an edge back to \(v\). This condition rules out the relevant short directed cycles through \(v\).

Their principal result is the inequality
\[
|\Gamma^{j}(v)|\geq |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1.
\]
In other words, at the \(j\)-th step the reachable set gains at least \(|\Gamma(v)|-1\) new vertices. By applying the estimate successively, one obtains the linear lower bound
\[
|\Gamma^{j}(v)|\geq 1+j\bigl(|\Gamma(v)|-1\bigr)
\]
whenever the corresponding no-short-return condition holds at each stage. The proof uses the symmetry of the relation to convert local expansion information at one vertex into a uniform global estimate.

This growth theorem has several consequences in additive and directed graph theory. It establishes Seymour’s conjectured neighborhood-growth bound for vertex-symmetric directed graphs. In the finite vertex-symmetric setting, the same estimate forces a short directed cycle and therefore proves the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture for this class of graphs. Interpreted through Cayley graphs and sumsets, the result also extends Shepherdson’s classical additive theorem: the expansion of iterated neighborhoods becomes a lower bound for repeated sums in a group. The work thus provides a common combinatorial framework for vertex-transitive graph growth, directed-cycle estimates, and additive expansion results.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a mathematics paper proving a growth inequality for powers of a point-symmetric reflexive relation, and mention applications to Seymour’s conjecture, the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture, and Shepherdson’s additive result.
counterfactuals.output:
We prove a sharp growth theorem for powers of a connected, point-symmetric reflexive relation \(\Gamma\). If \(\Gamma\) has finite valency \(d\), then for every point \(v\) and every integer \(k\ge 0\),
\[
|\Gamma^{k}(v)|\ge \min\bigl\{|V|,\;1+k(d-1)\bigr\}.
\]
Thus the iterated neighborhoods of a point grow at least linearly until they exhaust the underlying set. The proof uses the symmetry of the relation together with boundary and connectivity arguments, and includes the corresponding locally finite infinite case. As consequences, we obtain the point-transitive case of Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture and the standard vertex-transitive case of the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture. Applied to Cayley relations, the same inequality recovers Shepherdson’s classical lower bound for iterated sumsets.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: State the main theorem for a locally finite vertex-transitive reflexive directed graph under the condition \(\Gamma^j(v)\cap\Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\}\), then give its linear-growth corollary and key graph-theoretic applications.
counterfactuals.output:
Let \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) be a locally finite, vertex-transitive, reflexive directed graph, and write  
\[
\Gamma^0(v)=\{v\},\qquad \Gamma^j(v)=\Gamma(\Gamma^{j-1}(v)).
\]
Because \(\Gamma\) is reflexive, \(\Gamma^j(v)\) is the set of vertices reachable from \(v\) by a directed walk of length at most \(j\).

### Main theorem
If, for some \(j\ge 1\),
\[
\Gamma^j(v)\cap \Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\},
\]
then the \(j\)-th boundary satisfies
\[
\bigl|\Gamma^j(v)\setminus \Gamma^{j-1}(v)\bigr|
   \ge |\Gamma(v)|-1.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1.
\]

### Linear-growth corollary
The same hypothesis implies, by applying the theorem at every level \(1,\ldots ,j\),
\[
\boxed{\;|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge 1+j\bigl(|\Gamma(v)|-1\bigr).\;}
\]
Thus every layer before a return to an in-neighbor contains at least the loopless outdegree
\[
d=|\Gamma(v)|-1
\]
new vertices.

### Principal applications

1. **Girth bound for finite vertex-transitive digraphs.**  
   If the loopless outdegree is \(d\), the order is \(n\), and the directed girth is \(g\), then
   \[
   \boxed{\;n\ge 1+d(g-1).\;}
   \]
   Indeed, \(\Gamma^{g-2}(v)\) and \(\Gamma^{-}(v)\setminus\{v\}\) are disjoint, giving
   \[
   n\ge \bigl(1+d(g-2)\bigr)+d.
   \]

2. **Vertex-transitive case of the Caccetta–Häggkvist bound.**  
   The preceding inequality is equivalent to
   \[
   g\le \left\lceil\frac{n}{d}\right\rceil.
   \]
   Hence every finite vertex-transitive digraph of loopless outdegree \(d\) contains a directed cycle of length at most \(\lceil n/d\rceil\).

3. **Linear ball growth in infinite graphs.**  
   As long as no vertex reachable within \(j\) steps is an in-neighbor of \(v\), directed balls grow at least linearly:
   \[
   |\Gamma^j(v)|\ge 1+jd.
   \]
   In particular, a vertex-transitive digraph with no nontrivial directed return has at least linear volume growth.

4. **Cayley-graph and product-set consequences.**  
   For a group \(G\) and \(A\subseteq G\) with \(1\in A\), applying the theorem to the Cayley digraph gives
   \[
   A^j\cap A^{-1}=\{1\}
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   |A^j|\ge |A^{j-1}|+|A|-1,
   \]
   and hence
   \[
   |A^j|\ge 1+j(|A|-1).
   \]
   This is the graph-theoretic form of the Moser–Scherck–Kemperman–Wehn type product-growth phenomenon.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

This paper studies growth in iterated neighborhoods of a locally finite, reflexive, point-symmetric relation \(\Gamma\) on a set \(V\). Writing \(\Gamma^j(v)\) for the vertices reachable from \(v\) in at most \(j\) relational steps, symmetry ensures uniform local structure and yields an additive expansion estimate. At every nonsaturated stage,
\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1.
\]
Thus each iteration contributes at least \(|\Gamma(v)|-1\) new points, implying
\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge 1+j\bigl(|\Gamma(v)|-1\bigr)
\]
as long as the relevant neighborhoods remain finite and nonsaturated. The result extends classical sumset-growth principles to homogeneous relational structures and provides a basic tool for analyzing reachability, diameter, and expansion in vertex-transitive directed graphs.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how neighborhood growth in a vertex-symmetric graph can confirm Seymour’s conjecture and yield a short proof of the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture in the vertex-symmetric case.
counterfactuals.output:
Let \(D\) be a finite vertex-transitive digraph on \(n\) vertices, with constant out-degree \(d\). For a vertex \(v\), write

\[
L_i(v)=\{x:\operatorname{dist}_D(v,x)=i\}
\]

for its \(i\)-th out-distance layer. Thus \(L_1(v)=N^+(v)\), and \(L_2(v)\) is the second out-neighborhood in Seymour’s sense.

### Neighborhood-growth lemma

A standard isoperimetric result for vertex-transitive digraphs says that if the directed girth of \(D\) is \(g\), then

\[
|L_i(v)|\ge d \qquad (1\le i<g).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\bigl|\{x:\operatorname{dist}(v,x)\le r\}\bigr|
   \ge 1+rd,\qquad r<g.
\]

The reason is that, before a directed cycle can close, a distance layer cannot have boundary smaller than the first neighborhood. Vertex-transitivity lets one translate any hypothetical small-boundary set throughout the graph; the usual submodularity/atom argument then produces either a smaller such set or a directed cycle of length at most the layer number.

## Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture

Seymour’s conjecture states that every oriented graph has a vertex \(v\) such that

\[
|N^{++}(v)|\ge |N^+(v)|.
\]

If \(D\) is oriented, it has no directed \(2\)-cycle, so its directed girth satisfies \(g\ge3\). Applying the growth lemma with \(i=2\) gives, for every vertex \(v\),

\[
|N^{++}(v)|=|L_2(v)|\ge d=|N^+(v)|.
\]

Thus Seymour’s conjecture holds for vertex-transitive—or vertex-symmetric—oriented graphs, and in fact every vertex is a Seymour vertex.

## Caccetta–Häggkvist in the vertex-symmetric case

Let \(g\) be the directed girth. The layers

\[
L_0(v),L_1(v),\ldots,L_{g-1}(v)
\]

are disjoint, with \(|L_0(v)|=1\), and the growth lemma gives \(|L_i(v)|\ge d\) for \(1\le i<g\). Hence

\[
n\ge 1+(g-1)d.
\]

Therefore

\[
g\le 1+\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{d}\right\rfloor
   =\left\lceil\frac nd\right\rceil.
\]

So a vertex-symmetric digraph on \(n\) vertices with out-degree \(d\) contains a directed cycle of length at most

\[
\boxed{\left\lceil \frac nd\right\rceil},
\]

which is exactly the Caccetta–Häggkvist bound in the vertex-symmetric case. Both conclusions are therefore consequences of the same linear neighborhood-growth principle.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

\begin{abstract}
Let \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) be a reflexive, point-symmetric relation whose out-neighborhoods are finite, and write
\[
\Gamma(X)=\bigcup_{x\in X}\Gamma(x),\qquad
\Gamma^{-}(v)=\{x\in V:(x,v)\in E\}.
\]
We prove that, for every \(v\in V\) and integer \(j\ge 1\), the non-return condition
\[
\Gamma^{j}(v)\cap\Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\}
\]
implies the one-step expansion estimate
\[
\bigl|\Gamma^{j}(v)\bigr|
   \ge \bigl|\Gamma^{j-1}(v)\bigr|
      +\bigl|\Gamma(v)\bigr|-1.
\]
Since reflexivity gives
\(\Gamma^{i}(v)\subseteq\Gamma^{j}(v)\) for \(i\le j\), iteration yields
\[
\bigl|\Gamma^{j}(v)\bigr|
   \ge 1+\bigl(\lvert\Gamma(v)\rvert-1\bigr)j.
\]
For the Cayley relation associated with a finite subset \(A\) of a group, with identity \(0\in A\), one has
\(\Gamma^{j}(0)=jA\) and \(\Gamma^{-}(0)=-A\).  Thus the hypothesis
\(jA\cap(-A)=\{0\}\) gives
\[
|jA|\ge 1+j(|A|-1),
\]
recovering Shepherdson’s additive theorem as a special case of the relational expansion result.
\end{abstract}
